name: Third-Party and Supply Chain Risk
blurb: Models, datasets, packages, MCP servers, and vendor AI features as an attack surface: provenance, AI bills of materials, and the fourth parties nobody assessed.

topics.body: Indirect injection arrives through content your organization never wrote: a vendor's document, a partner's web page, a shared inbox, a third-party MCP server's tool descriptions. Every external content source an AI system reads is now part of the supply chain, and vendor assessment has to ask questions questionnaires never covered, including how retrieved third-party content is isolated from instructions, and whether the vendor's own AI features read content your adversaries can write.
topics.name: Prompt Injection
topics.blurb: Direct and indirect prompt injection: how instructions hidden in content hijack model behavior, documented attacks, and current defenses.

topics.body: Poisoning enters through the supply chain more often than through your own pipeline: a pretrained model with a planted backdoor, a public dataset seeded with corrupted samples, a fine-tune performed by a party you never assessed. Research collected in NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy shows small fractions of poisoned training data can implant reliable trigger behavior. Provenance is the control: know where every model and dataset came from, prefer sources with integrity guarantees, and treat an unverifiable lineage as a finding rather than an unknown.
topics.name: Model and Data Poisoning
topics.blurb: Corrupting training data or model weights to plant backdoors and biases, and the research on detecting it.

topics.body: The AI supply chain mutates weekly while assessment cycles run annually, and the annual questionnaire cannot survive that mismatch. Your vendor is the third party, but the foundation model their product runs on is a fourth party, the fine-tuning shop is another, and the hosting infrastructure may be a fifth, none of them visible in the questionnaire, the contract, or the assessment. An AI bill of materials, disclosing the models, datasets, and services a product depends on, is the instrument that makes the invisible chain assessable, and continuous external monitoring replaces the point-in-time attestation that was stale before it was signed.
topics.name: AI Supply Chain Attacks
topics.blurb: Compromised models, datasets, and packages upstream: malicious model files, dependency attacks, opaque fourth-party model chains, AI bills of materials, and registry integrity.

topics.body: Every shadow tool is a vendor relationship nobody assessed, complete with terms nobody read, data-processing commitments nobody negotiated, and subprocessors nobody knows exist. Folding discovered tools into the vendor process, even retroactively, is how the third-party program regains contact with reality.
topics.name: Shadow AI
topics.blurb: Unsanctioned AI use inside organizations: the exposure it creates and how enterprises detect and govern it.

topics.body: KYC and identity-proofing vendors are the outsourced front line, and their resistance to synthetic media is now an assessable property: how their liveness checks perform against current generation tools, how quickly they update against new techniques, and what they disclose about bypass rates belongs in the assessment of any vendor whose product decides who gets an account.
topics.name: Deepfakes and Synthetic Identity
topics.blurb: Synthetic media fraud, identity spoofing, detection methods, and the laws responding to them.

topics.body: Supply chain tooling makes model provenance checkable: scanners that inspect model files for embedded code, AI bill-of-materials generators, registry security controls, and signing infrastructure for datasets and model artifacts. The gap this category fills is that classic software-composition analysis never learned to read a model file, and the tools that do are the difference between a disclosed model chain and an opaque one.
topics.name: AI Security Tooling
topics.blurb: The defensive tooling landscape, organized by six security domains: Security Governance and Risk Management, Security Operations, Architecture and Engineering, Application and Product Security, Third-Party and Supply Chain Risk, and Data Protection and Privacy.

topics.body: Third-party agents and the MCP servers they connect through are a new vendor class arriving faster than assessment categories can form, and this site tracks the registry ecosystem at the scale of nearly two thousand servers. Assessing them means asking about tool provenance, what hidden context and instructions ship with the integration, and how authority attenuates when your agent delegates to a vendor's agent across an organizational boundary.
topics.name: AI Agent Security
topics.blurb: Agent kill chains, cascading multi-agent failure, circuit breakers, agent-to-agent trust boundaries, and runtime supervision of autonomous systems.

topics.body: Red-team requirements belong in AI vendor contracts: what adversarial testing the vendor performs, on what cadence, whether results or summaries are shareable, and whether your own testing of their product is permitted. A vendor that cannot answer those questions is asking you to inherit an untested attack surface on faith.
topics.name: AI Red Teaming and Adversarial Evaluation
topics.blurb: Continuous adversarial testing of AI systems: methods, benchmarks, disclosure practices, and the evidence that earns expanded autonomy.

topics.body: Every assistant, model API and package in the pipeline is a supplier. Vendor risk teams assess the coding assistants themselves, what they retain and train on, and increasingly ask software suppliers for SSDF attestations and software bills of materials before buying.
topics.name: Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)
topics.blurb: Building security into every phase of how software is planned, written, tested and shipped, and what changes when AI writes the code and AI features ship in the product.

topics.body: MCP servers, plugins, model providers and the packages agents install are third parties the agent reaches on its own. Vendor risk has to assess them before an agent is allowed to, and treat an unreviewed MCP server with the same suspicion as any unvetted software.
topics.name: Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC) Security
topics.blurb: The security risks of building, deploying and running autonomous AI agents: tool and MCP bridges, prompt attacks on dynamic input, agent-made supply chain risk, and failures at machine speed.

program.body: An annual questionnaire cannot govern a supply chain that changes weekly. Volume VI's illustrative scenario makes the point: a program got satisfactory answers from 94 percent of its Tier 1 vendors, and three months later found seven of them had shipped undisclosed AI features, two touching data that required extra controls. The questionnaire was not wrong; it was obsolete. The replacement is continuous monitoring: every Tier 1 vendor watched for breach disclosures, privacy policy changes, model-provider switches and AI feature announcements; every Tier 1 contract reviewed against an AI clause library; and every new AI vendor required to submit a bill of materials before the contract is signed. The number to show the CISO is vendors assessed continuously right now, not vendors assessed last year.
program.name: Vendor Risk Assessments

program.body: An AI bill of materials sits beside the software bill of materials and records what a model was built from and runs on: training data sources, base model, fine-tuning datasets, third-party libraries, the model providers and subprocessors in the chain, and the data flows. Buyers should make it a condition of contract execution, refreshed on every material change; vendors should produce it in that form so it arrives complete rather than assembled under deadline. Inside the enterprise, the same record belongs in a model registry: every AI system, model version, agent, external AI connection and associated non-human identity. When a vulnerability is disclosed in a component, the bill of materials is how you find everything it touched.
program.name: Machine Learning Bill of Materials

program.body: Downloading weights from a public hub is importing executable risk. Nearly 45 percent of popular models on the largest public hub still use a serialization format that runs code when loaded, and scanners miss most loading paths, so Volume VII does not rely on scanners. It sets admission conditions instead: a license compatible with the lineage of the data the model was trained on, since a permissive model tuned on a non-commercial dataset carries the dataset's terms; provenance and a signature traceable to a publisher; a safe load path; and an owner. For any model in use, the enterprise should know the hash of the served artifact and be able to verify it has not changed.

program.body: Lineage is a legal fact as much as a technical one: a permissively licensed model tuned on a non-commercially licensed dataset carries the dataset's terms, so license compatibility has to be checked against the lineage of what the model was trained on. The same check belongs in acquisitions: model provenance and licenses against dataset lineage, and whose data the models were trained or tuned on, under what terms. After deployment, lineage extends to decisions: someone must own the record of what the AI system did and why, retained and organized so it can answer an incident team, a regulator or a plaintiff's attorney when a decision is challenged.

program.body: For a service consumed through an API, the question is not uptime but who is responsible for what, and what changes without notice. Volume IX draws a Shared Responsibility Line for AI systems, and the Cloud Security Alliance now models that responsibility across four parties: the cloud provider, the model provider, the orchestrated service provider and the application provider. A consumed model also cannot be audited from inside, so the boundaries and limits around it carry the load, and the provider's silent updates remain the standing threat: the model behind the endpoint can change and alter behaviour that was tested. The contractual counterpart is a model-change notification clause.

program.body: Poisoned components sit at the foundation of the AI supply chain, above any vendor relationship and outside assessment reach: compromised open models, malicious weights in public repositories, and backdoored datasets that plant behavior in every model trained on them. A vendor's questionnaire will not capture them, because the vendor is as blind to them as you are. Backdoors pass pre-deployment testing because the trigger never occurs in the test. Volume VII names the result a behavioral vulnerability, a way to make the product act outside its intended authority without any code defect, and gives it a reporting and response procedure of its own, like any other vulnerability class.

program.body: Most AI vendor capability runs on a small number of foundation model providers, so a vendor portfolio that looks diverse hides a concentration that no tier map shows. Ask a vendor which model powers a feature and the answer is often that it is proprietary or varies by workload. That fourth-party risk, carried by vendors' vendors and the model providers behind them, currently falls between the CISO's supply chain responsibility and the chief data officer's model governance, and neither owns it fully. Volume VI's advice is to claim it deliberately before a regulator assigns it, and to ask the fourth-party question of every Tier 1 vendor now.

program.body: Contract review for AI works against a clause library: provisions required, prohibited or monitored across every AI vendor agreement. Required clauses include a ban on using enterprise data for model training without explicit written consent, model-change notification, AI incident disclosure and audit rights. The better programs are retrofitting AI addenda onto active Tier 1 master agreements, which creates obligations and standing that did not exist before. Findings are routed by severity: a missing addendum in a low-tier contract waits for renewal, while a Tier 1 clause that permits training on enterprise data goes to the General Counsel within 24 hours.
program.name: Contractual Security Requirements

program.body: Some AI risk is bought rather than built. Purchased software is adding model features every release, on by default, configured by the vendor and fed by the enterprise's own data: the document platform that summarizes reads every file, the ticketing system that drafts replies reads every ticket. When a whole product or company is acquired, Volume VII's diligence checklist asks for model provenance and licenses checked against dataset lineage, training data rights, evidence that adversarial behavior was ever measured, and the default authority the product's agents hold. Data derived by inference counts too: health status inferred from purchases is health data, even though nobody collected it.
program.name: Auditing Acquired Data
program.note: Security audits of datasets bought from data brokers are not treated separately.

program.body: The enterprise often learns of a vendor incident late: disclosures appear in regulatory filings, press releases and breach notification databases before the vendor contacts customers. Monitoring those sources in real time means third-party risk knows the day it is disclosed, not the week the vendor calls. Response then follows the AI incident sequence, with one step that dominates in the supply chain: propagation scoping, finding every agent that consumed the compromised component's output and every knowledge base that ingested it. For product vendors, Volume VII adds machine-readable advisories, a bill of materials and an exploitability statement that customers' tools can match without a human.
